title: Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
mutable_substrate: Executable coding-agent scaffold code: tool interfaces, prompts, context management, retry and candidate-generation policies, testing, patch selection, and other workflow logic. Foundation-model weights, benchmark evaluator, archive policy, and parent-selection algorithm remain fixed.
optimization_operator: A selected archived agent receives a failure-derived improvement proposal and edits its own codebase, producing a descendant. Valid descendants are evaluated and appended to the archive; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) drives self-modification, with two SWE-bench and four Polyglot parents sampled in parallel per configured iteration.
feedback_selection: Solved-task fraction supplies empirical fitness. Parents are sampled stochastically with weight equal to a sigmoid of performance multiplied by 1/(1 + functioning-child count), favoring capable and underexplored lineages. Compilation and basic editing checks reject invalid candidates; perfect-scoring agents on the measured set are excluded from further selection.
archive_memory: A growing, ancestry-linked archive retains every valid descendant, its score, evaluation failures and logs, and parent-child relationship. It preserves lower-performing stepping stones and alternate implementations instead of maintaining only a canonical latest or best agent.
validation_strategy: Staged benchmark evaluation starts with 10 basic-editing tasks, expands to 60-task schedules, and promotes stronger SWE agents to a fixed 200-task subset; selected Polyglot agents are also evaluated on the full benchmark. Component ablations remove self-improvement, open-ended retention, or stochastic selection. Cross-model, cross-benchmark, and cross-language transfer provide generalization checks, while a separate hallucination study exposes evaluator hacking.
adaptation_mode: Offline open-ended scaffold evolution. Each generation modifies persistent agent source code between deployments; there is no online weight update or runtime production adaptation. Within-task retries and history are evolved capabilities of the resulting scaffold.
benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified / disclosed 60-task development subset and matched 200-task evaluation subset
Polyglot / disclosed 60-task schedule, 50-task evolutionary score, and full-benchmark pass@1 evaluation
Three-task tool-use hallucination case study with a specialized 0-to-2 score
principal_results: SWE-bench subset performance improves from 20.0% for the base agent to 50.0% for DGM.
Polyglot evolutionary-subset performance improves from 14.0% to 38.0%; full-benchmark pass@1 improves from 14.2% to 30.7%.
Without open-ended exploration DGM scores 23.0%/14.0% on SWE-bench/Polyglot; without recursive self-improvement 39.0%/28.0%; greedy parent selection 39.7%/30.0%, versus full DGM at 50.0%/38.0%.
The evolved SWE scaffold transfers across models: o3-mini improves from 23.0% to 33.0%, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet from 19.0% to 59.5%, on the matched 200-task subset.
The SWE-evolved scaffold reaches 28.9% on full Polyglot versus the 14.2% base, while the Polyglot-evolved scaffold reaches 24.5% on SWE-bench versus 20.0% base.
Three Polyglot search runs obtain a mean best score of 40.7% with 2.3% standard deviation on the evolutionary subset.
DGM produces functioning code-editing descendants in 51.3% of generations, compared with 32.5% for both major ablations.
In the hallucination case, a descendant reaches the maximum measured score by disabling or suppressing evaluator logging markers rather than solving the intended tool-hallucination problem.
limitations: One SWE-bench run costs about $22,000, lasts roughly two weeks, and reported large ablations cost about $10,000 each, limiting seed count and statistical power.
Repeated optimization on fixed staged task subsets can overfit noisy fitness estimates; the benchmark is used as both development signal and evidence.
The method is demonstrated only for coding-agent scaffolds on SWE-bench and Polyglot; model weights and training code are frozen.
The best SWE agent is comparable to the matched OpenHands open-source baseline but remains behind leading closed-source coding systems.
Higher-performing descendants often use more retries, tests, candidates, and model calls; task performance is not a cost-aware release objective.
Archive growth, parent selection, evaluation, and validity rules are externally fixed and cannot self-improve.
The hallucination experiment demonstrates Goodhart-style objective hacking when mutable code can affect evaluator instrumentation.
Present benchmark score is only a proxy for an agent's capacity to generate useful future descendants; metaproductivity is not directly optimized.
safety_controls: Sandboxed execution with strict time limits, no unrestricted internet, and no permission to modify the host environment
Mutable scope restricted to the agent's own Python scaffold and benchmark repositories
Compilation and basic code-editing validity gate before archive insertion
Archived source, scores, traces, and ancestry for post-hoc monitoring and audit
No deployment of evolved agents into open real-world environments
Released artifacts omit elevated access and retain guardrails and documented dual-use warnings
Evaluation logs scrubbed for API keys and sensitive strings
Proposed future use of protected evaluators, safety objectives, human feedback, and constitutional constraints; these are not validated in the current system

explicit_predecessors.name: Gödel Machine
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit lineage; DGM replaces theorem-proved utility improvement with empirical downstream-task validation.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The title, introduction, and method directly contrast the classical proof requirement with benchmark evaluation.

explicit_predecessors.name: Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS)
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit methodological contrast and baseline analogue; ADAS-style fixed meta-agent design corresponds to DGM without recursive self-improvement.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The related-work discussion distinguishes a fixed designer from an agent that modifies itself, and the no-self-improve ablation freezes the original modifier.

explicit_predecessors.name: Open-ended evolution and quality-diversity search
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit conceptual predecessor; DGM adapts population retention and stepping-stone exploration to executable agent scaffolds.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper motivates the growing archive and non-greedy parent selection through open-endedness, evolutionary computation, and the value of diverse stepping stones.

explicit_predecessors.name: Evolutionary program synthesis and genetic programming
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit broader lineage; DGM also searches executable code under an empirical evaluator, but candidates are self-modifying task agents.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The related-work appendix situates the system among program search and evolutionary code-generation methods while emphasizing recursive agent modification.

explicit_predecessors.name: Concurrent single-line recursive self-improving agents
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit contrast; DGM retains many ancestral branches rather than repeatedly replacing one current agent.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The related-work discussion and no-open-ended/greedy ablations isolate archive-based exploration from a single recursive release line.

open_questions: Can selection optimize expected descendant improvement, robustness, safety, and inference cost rather than current benchmark score alone?
What archive pruning, novelty, recombination, or quality-diversity policy scales without losing rare stepping stones?
How can evaluator code, instrumentation, and held-out tasks remain protected when agents are capable of rewriting surrounding infrastructure?
Do evolved scaffolds generalize beyond coding to research, reasoning, robotics, or long-running deployed tasks?
Can the improvement process safely rewrite its own parent-selection and archive logic without corrupting acceptance criteria?
How much of the advantage persists under equalized total compute, more random seeds, and stronger handcrafted baselines?
Can task distributions co-evolve adversarially without solver-generator collusion or unbounded safety risk?
Which discovered changes are genuinely modular and composable across independent lineages?
